Cycle: Chapter one. What a cycle is.

First, what is a business cycle? In 1946, Arthur Burns and Wesley Mitchell defined it as expansions that happen at about the same time in many economic activities, followed by similarly general contractions: recurrent, but not periodic, and lasting from more than a year to ten or twelve years. Here is America's real output since 1947, on a log scale, so that a straight line is steady growth. The grey bands are the recessions dated by the committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research that Burns and Mitchell built: 12 of them. Look how small they are against the growth. The cycle is a wobble around a trend, and to measure the wobble you first need the trend.

The most used trend in macroeconomics was proposed by Robert Hodrick and Edward Prescott, in a paper circulated from 1980 and published in 1997. Choose a trend tau to make two things small at once: the gaps between the data and the trend, and the changes in the trend's slope. The first term keeps the trend close to the data. The second keeps it smooth. Lambda sets the balance, and for quarterly data everyone uses sixteen hundred, a convention rather than an estimate. Here is the trend through log output, in gold. Subtract it and what is left is the cycle: output's percentage gap from trend. Its standard deviation is 1.6 percent, and every recession shows as a dip.

Not everyone accepts the convention. In 2018 James Hamilton published a paper called Why You Should Never Use the Hodrick-Prescott Filter. He showed it can create cyclical patterns that are not in the data, and that its estimate near the end of the sample keeps changing as new data arrive. His alternative: define the cycle as the error you make when you forecast output two years ahead by a regression on its last four quarters. Whatever you could not have seen coming is the cycle. In red, Hamilton's cycle; in green, Hodrick and Prescott's. They agree about timing, with a correlation of 0.73, but Hamilton's swings are twice the size: 3.2 percent against 1.6. How big the cycle is depends on how you define the trend, and so does every number a model is asked to match.

Here is the end-point problem at work. In gold, the Hodrick-Prescott cycle for 2000 to 2008, computed with only the data available up to the third quarter of 2008. It puts that quarter 1.8 percent below trend: the trend carries on at the pace of the boom years, and output has fallen short of it. In green, the same quarters filtered with all the data we have today, including the recession and the slow recovery that followed. Now the same quarter is 1.3 percent above trend, because the trend has bent down to meet the years after. Near the end of a sample, the trend is a guess about data that have not arrived. So the most recent cycle, the one a policymaker cares about, is the one any filter measures worst; here even its sign flipped.

With a filter in hand, the cycle becomes a table of numbers, and this table is what any model of the cycle is asked to explain. America, 1948 to 2019, before the pandemic. Output's cycle has a standard deviation of 1.6 percent. Consumer spending moves less, 0.77 times as much, and that includes cars and other durables. Investment moves 4.6 times as much as output: it is where the cycle lives. Hours worked move almost as much as output, and with it. Output per hour moves about half as much, with a correlation of only 0.44. Hold on to these numbers: in chapter nine the model gets its own column.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: which one turns first?

Your turn. Here are six American series around the peak of a business cycle, the quarter the NBER says the expansion ended, marked by the dashed line. Each is the average over the ten recessions from 1953 to 2007, measured as a percentage from where the series stood at the peak, with its normal growth taken out. They include real output, consumer spending, business investment, housing investment, hours worked and output per hour, in some order. Which one turns down first, well before the recession begins? Pause, and choose a letter.

The answer is C: housing investment. On average it reached its high about 7 quarters before the peak of the cycle, and fell 21 percent below that high within a year after it. Output, hours and business investment turn together, about two quarters before the peak, and business investment then falls furthest and longest. Consumer spending flattens a little earlier. And output per hour does something interesting: it stalls well before the peak, dips as the recession starts, and then recovers while hours are still falling.

In 2007, at the Federal Reserve's Jackson Hole symposium, Edward Leamer gave a paper with the title Housing Is the Business Cycle. Housing is the kind of spending most sensitive to interest rates and to credit. It turns first because monetary policy and credit conditions turn first. Keep that in mind, because the model this part builds is driven by technology alone, and in a world driven only by technology there is no reason for houses to lead. It is a clue, and it comes back in chapter eleven, and in the next two parts.
Cake: Chapter three. Dynamic programming: the cake.

Before an economy with shocks, a much smaller problem, which contains the whole method. You have a cake of size one, and it has to last for ever. Each day you choose how much to eat, and you want to make the discounted sum of your enjoyment as large as possible, subject to never eating more cake than there is. Eat some today, and save the rest. Your patience is 0.9: a slice tomorrow is worth 0.9 of the same slice today. Enjoyment is the logarithm of what you eat, so the first bite of a day is worth the most, and a day with nothing at all is a disaster. Written like this, it is a choice of infinitely many numbers at once, far too many to search.

Richard Bellman's trick, from the 1950s, is to stop thinking about the whole path. Let V of w be the best you can do, in total, starting with a cake of size w. Then V of w is the best choice of today's slice, c, of today's enjoyment, plus beta times the best you can do from tomorrow on, starting with what is left, w minus c. That is the Bellman equation. It rests on what Bellman called the principle of optimality: whatever you do today, an optimal plan must behave optimally from tomorrow on, given where today left you. The infinite choice has become one choice and one number, at the price of an unknown function, V, that appears on both sides.

For this problem the unknown function can be found by hand. Guess that V is a constant plus some number b times the log of the cake. Then today's choice must balance the last bite eaten today, one over c, against the value of saving it, beta b over what is left. That gives c as w over one plus beta b. Put this back into the equation and match the terms in log w on both sides: b must equal one plus beta b, so b is one over one minus beta. And the rule is beautifully simple: eat one minus beta of whatever is left. With patience 0.9, eat 10 percent of the cake every day, for ever. The rule is a policy function: it tells you what to do in every state you could find yourself in, not just along one path.

Here is the plan in action. The pale bars are the cake at the start of each day. The bright ones are what you eat: 10 percent of it. After twenty days, 0.12 of the cake remains. It never runs out: it shrinks by a tenth a day, for ever, and consumption shrinks with it. Most problems in this part cannot be solved by hand, so the next chapter does it the way a computer does, and the cake is the test that the computer gets right.
VFI: A computer cannot guess the shape of V. It does something simpler. Put the cake sizes on a grid, here 1,001 of them, and start from any guess at all, say V is zero everywhere. Then apply the Bellman equation as a recipe: today's best choice, valued with yesterday's guess, gives a new guess. The guesses have a meaning. V n is the best you can do if the world ends after n days. V one: eat everything today. V two, V five, V ten: each is lower, because the cake must stretch over more days. By V one hundred, nothing moves any more. And the dashed line is the exact answer found by hand. The iterations land on it, except at the smallest cakes, where a grid of thousandths is too coarse to cut.

Why must this work? Call the recipe T: it takes a guess V and returns a new one. Take any two guesses. After one application of T, the largest distance between them has shrunk by at least the factor beta. Here is the distance between successive guesses for the cake, on a log scale. It falls on a straight line, by a factor of 0.90 at each step, which is beta exactly. David Blackwell showed in 1965 that two plain properties are enough for this: more cake tomorrow is never worse, and the future is discounted. A map that shrinks distances like this is a contraction, and a contraction has exactly one fixed point, which the iterations reach from any starting guess. Here it takes 238 steps to agree to ten decimal places. That guarantee is why economists can solve problems with no pencil-and-paper answer at all.

The value function is only a means. What you want is the policy: how much to eat with each size of cake. The dots are the computer's policy, read off the grid as the best choice at each point. The line is the exact rule, one minus beta of the cake. On average the computer eats 10.4 percent instead of ten, because on this grid the cake can only be cut in thousandths. Finer grids, interpolation between grid points, or smarter methods close the gap. Value function iteration is slow but almost impossible to break, and it is the method the rest of this part builds on.
Growth: Chapter five. The stochastic growth model.

Now replace the cake with an economy. Output is made from capital, k, with a technology level, z, that changes at random. Each year the economy splits output between eating and next year's capital, and the Bellman equation now has two states, capital and technology, and an expectation over next year's luck. William Brock and Leonard Mirman studied this model in 1972. With log utility and capital that is used up within the year, it has a closed form: save a share alpha beta of output, 0.35, whatever happens, and eat the rest. Here is a century of it on the Island. In red, technology. In green, output. A good year raises output, and because a fixed share is saved, it also raises next year's capital, so output's swings last longer than technology's. Capital is the model's propagation mechanism.

A computer cannot hold a continuous random variable, so technology is squeezed onto a few values, with a table of probabilities for moving between them: a Markov chain. Here are four such tables, each with seven states. A row is today's state, a column tomorrow's, and a brighter square a likelier move. The aim is to copy a process with persistence 0.95, whose true standard deviation is 2.24 percent. George Tauchen's method of 1986, the old standard, gets 2.77 percent and a persistence of 0.962: close, but off. The method of Geert Rouwenhorst, revived by Kopecky and Suen in 2010, matches both exactly. And when persistence is very high, at 0.995, Tauchen's chain breaks altogether: its states are so far apart that it never moves, while Rouwenhorst's is still exact. Small numerical choices like this decide whether a solved model means anything.

Now solve the growth model the way the computer solved the cake: a grid for capital, a chain for technology, and value function iteration. First the test. With capital used up each year, the grid's policy is within 0.44 percent of Brock and Mirman's formula, less than one step of the grid. Then the real case: capital lasts, with a tenth wearing out each year, and there is no formula. Here is how much capital grows, against how much there is, one line for each of five technology states, from bad in red to good in green. Each line crosses zero where capital would stay the same: with good luck the economy builds towards more capital, with bad luck it runs capital down towards less. The computer took 409 iterations and did not care that no formula exists. That is the power of the method.
Labour: Chapter six. Why work more in a boom?

The model so far has no labour. But in the data, hours worked swing almost as much as output, so a model of the cycle must say why people work more in booms. Give the household a dislike of working, n hours, with a parameter phi that sets how strongly the dislike rises with hours. In a boom, productivity and so the wage are temporarily high. The smart response is to work now and rest later, when work pays less. Robert Lucas and Leonard Rapping proposed this in 1969: it is the logic of a fisherman who fishes hardest when the fish are running. Phi measures it: the percentage change in hours for a one percent change in a temporary wage, called the Frisch elasticity after Ragnar Frisch. A permanent rise does much less, because people who are richer for good also want more leisure, and the two pulls roughly cancel.

How big is phi? Here is the whole model of this part, solved again for each value. Across the bottom, the Frisch elasticity, on a log scale; up the side, how much hours move relative to output. In the data, hours move 0.90 times as much as output. Studies of individual workers find elasticities somewhere around a quarter to four fifths: the blue band. With phi at a half, the model's hours move only 0.24 times as much as output: a cycle in which hardly anyone changes how much they work. To get even halfway to the data, the model needs phi of about 2.1, far above what workers' own records show. This is the central weakness of the theory, and the next idea is the attempt to fix it.

Richard Rogerson and Gary Hansen found a way around the problem. Most jobs come as a full shift or nothing: you work forty hours a week or you do not work. So an economy adjusts mostly by changing how many people work, not how long each person works. Here are sixty people in a normal quarter. In a boom, a few more are at work; in a slump, a few fewer. Rogerson showed that if people can insure themselves against being the one who is not hired, the whole economy behaves as if a single household had an infinite Frisch elasticity. Hansen put this into the growth model in 1985, and hours now move 0.76 times as much as output, against 0.90 in the data. Each person's elasticity is zero, and the economy's is infinite. The Island uses Hansen's version from here on. Whether this is a solution or a trick is still argued, and it is this part's dial.
Calibrate: The model has a handful of numbers to choose. Kydland and Prescott's rule was to take them from facts that have nothing to do with the cycle, and only then ask the model about the cycle. Capital's share alpha comes from the share of income paid to labour: in the Penn World Table it averaged 0.62 for America from 1950 to 2019, so alpha is about 0.38. The Island uses the classic 0.36. Patience comes from the real interest rate. At about four percent a year, beta is 0.99 a quarter. Depreciation is a choice about what counts as capital. The table's rate, 3.6 percent a year, includes houses and buildings that last a century; the Island takes the textbook two and a half percent a quarter, for machinery. Hours: Americans worked about 1,884 hours a year, roughly a third of their waking time. And technology's persistence and the size of its shocks come from the measured Solow residual, which chapter ten examines.

With the numbers chosen, the model's long-run state follows from three equations. In the steady state the Euler equation says the return on capital must just repay impatience and wear, which fixes the ratio of capital to output. Investment must replace what wears out. And the hours condition sets the weight on leisure, A, so that people work a third of their time. The Island holds 10.3 quarters of output as capital, 2.6 years, less than the table's 3.6 because its capital wears out faster. It invests 26 percent of output, close to the data's 24, and consumes the rest. The long-run facts are matched by construction. The test is whether the short-run facts, which were never targeted, come out right.

Calibration started a long argument. On one side, Kydland and Prescott, writing in 1996: every model is deliberately false, so it should not be judged by a statistical test it is bound to fail. Match the long-run facts, borrow numbers from studies of growth and of individuals, and judge the model on facts it was not built to match. On the other, Lars Peter Hansen and James Heckman, in the same issue of the same journal: without standard errors, a good fit may be luck; a number measured on individuals need not apply to a whole economy, as the Frisch elasticity shows; and the honest procedure is to choose all the numbers to fit all the data. The argument ended in a compromise. Modern models are estimated as a whole, by likelihood, with prior beliefs about the parameters that carry the calibrator's knowledge. Part fifty-five does it.
Linear: Chapter eight. Solving the model: the saddle path.

Value function iteration works, but with capital, technology and hours it gets slow, and real models have many more variables. The standard alternative starts from the conditions an equilibrium must satisfy. First, saving: giving up a unit of consumption today must pay, in expectation, as much as it costs, through capital's return. Second, work: the wage an extra hour earns must buy exactly what the hour costs in leisure. Third, building: whatever is not eaten becomes next quarter's capital. Fourth, luck: technology wanders at random, drifting back towards normal. Four equations, holding for every quarter, with an expectation of the future inside.

Next, make the system linear. Measure every variable as its percentage gap from the steady state, the hats, and replace each equation by its first-order Taylor expansion. Near the steady state, the whole economy becomes one matrix equation. Here it is for the Island, with the numbers the computer found by differentiating the four conditions. Hours and output have been eliminated: given capital, technology and consumption, the labour condition pins them down. Notice the difference between the variables. Capital and technology are given at the start of each quarter: they are predetermined. Consumption is chosen, and can jump to anything. The solution must say how.

How does the matrix decide? Through its roots, the generalized eigenvalues of the two matrices, which say how fast each combination of gaps grows or shrinks. The Island's system has three. Two lie inside the unit circle: combinations that shrink each quarter, towards the steady state. One lies outside, at about one point oh seven: a combination that grows seven percent a quarter, for ever, if it is ever set off. Olivier Blanchard and Charles Kahn proved in 1980 that such a system has exactly one stable solution when the number of unstable roots equals the number of variables free to jump. Here there is one of each: one unstable root, and consumption. Consumption must jump to the one value that keeps the explosive combination at exactly zero. Counting roots tells you whether a model has an answer, and how many.

Here is what the unstable root means. Start the Island with capital twenty percent below normal, and try five different choices of consumption. Eat too little, and capital piles up past any sensible level, with consumption eventually collapsing. Eat too much, and capital runs out. Only one choice leads into the steady state: the saddle path. A rational household, looking ahead, chooses it. The computer finds it exactly. Consumption's gap is 0.53 times capital's gap plus 0.47 times technology's. And capital's gap shrinks by a factor of 0.942 a quarter, the stable root from before. Paul Klein's method of 2000 does this for any number of variables, using a matrix factorization called QZ, and it is inside every modern model-solving package.
Responses: Chapter nine. The model beside the data.

Now the model's answer. Technology on the Island improves by one percent, and the improvement fades by five percent a quarter. Output jumps by 1.9 percent, almost twice the shock, because people also work more: hours rise 1.5 percent. Consumption rises only 0.47 percent at first, and keeps rising for three years, while the wage moves with it exactly. Investment takes the windfall: up 6.2 percent on impact. Every series moves together, and in the right order of size.

Each line has a reason. The household knows the good times will fade, so it does not spend the gain at once; it spreads it over years. That is consumption smoothing, from Part twenty-two. So the windfall goes into capital, and investment swings hardest. The wage is temporarily high, so now is the time to work: intertemporal substitution. With Hansen's indivisible labour, the labour condition says the wage equals A times consumption, so it can only move as slowly as consumption does. And the extra capital keeps output up after the shock has faded: capital peaks after 18 quarters.

Now the test Prescott proposed: simulate the Island for twenty thousand quarters, filter the result exactly as the data were filtered, and put its numbers beside America's. The size of the cycle: 1.8 percent against 1.6. Close, from shocks sized only by the Solow residual. Consumption: the model's is far too smooth, though the data here include cars and other durables. Investment: about three times as volatile as output, against four and a half. The right order. Hours: 0.76 against 0.90, thanks to Hansen. Output per hour: too smooth. And the worst miss: in the model, hours and output per hour move together, with a correlation of 0.76. In the data, there is no correlation at all. Persistence: close. A model with one shock and no frictions gets the broad shape of the cycle. That is what impressed people. The misses are where the next chapters dig.
Fit: Chapter ten. What fits and what does not.

Start with the worst miss. On the left, every quarter of American data: hours worked against output per hour, both as gaps from trend. On the right, the Island. In the model, the only shock is technology, which raises both the productivity of an hour and the desire to work, so the dots line up: a correlation of 0.76. In America, the cloud has no slope at all: minus 0.07. Lawrence Christiano and Martin Eichenbaum made this the central puzzle in 1992. Hours must also be moved by something that shifts labour supply, not demand: in their paper, government spending. A model with a single shock gets one line, and the data are a cloud.

The picture also changed over time. Split the sample in the mid-1980s. Before, output per hour rose and fell with output, with a correlation of 0.64, which is what Kydland and Prescott saw. Since then, the correlation with output is about zero, minus 0.10, and with hours it is strongly negative, minus 0.59. At the same time the whole cycle calmed: output's standard deviation fell from 2.0 to 1.0 percent, the Great Moderation. In recent recessions, firms cut hours hard and kept their most productive work, so productivity held up as hours fell. A theory in which productivity drives the cycle fitted the data it was built on better than the data that came after.

Now the shocks themselves. The model's technology is measured by the Solow residual of Part twenty: output growth minus the growth that capital and hours account for, weighted by their shares of income. Here it is for America, year by year, from the Penn World Table. And output's growth, in green. They move together: the cycles have a correlation of 0.80. This was Prescott's evidence that technology drives the cycle. But look at the red bars: 6 years in which measured technology went backwards. In 1982, it fell 1.6 percent. Did America forget how to make things in 1982, in the middle of a recession caused, by almost every account, by the Federal Reserve's high interest rates?

The residual measures more than technology. In a slump, firms hold on to workers they do not fully use, because hiring and training are costly: labour hoarding. Machines run fewer shifts, but the measured capital stock does not fall. So measured productivity falls whenever demand falls, whatever happens to technology, and its correlation with output proves little. The pattern can even reverse: in 2009, output fell, but the residual rose 0.5 percent, because firms shed workers faster than output fell. Susanto Basu, John Fernald and Miles Kimball built a measure of technology corrected for utilization and published it in 2006. In their corrected series, when technology improves, hours and investment fall at first, and output barely moves: the opposite of the model's prediction. The shocks the theory needed were partly an artefact of measurement.
Critics: The first sharp critique came in 1986, in the same issue of the Minneapolis Fed's Quarterly Review that carried Prescott's case. Lawrence Summers called it some skeptical observations. The parameters: the labour-supply response the theory needs is far larger than what studies of workers find, as chapter six showed. The shocks: what are they? Where is the evidence that technology goes backwards in recessions? Prices: the theory predicts how wages and interest rates should move, and those predictions had not been checked. And exchange: in the Depression, markets and banks broke down, and a theory without money, credit or failures has nothing to say about that. Prescott's reply, in the same issue, was that theory was ahead of measurement: better data would come round.

The decisive test came from Jordi Galí in 1999. Instead of measuring technology with the Solow residual, let the data say what a technology shock is. Fit a statistical model to two series together, the growth of output per hour and hours worked: a vector autoregression. Then call a technology shock whatever moves productivity for ever. This is Blanchard and Quah's long-run restriction, from 1989. The logic: a fall in demand can lower measured productivity for a while, as firms hoard labour, but only technology can change it permanently. Having found the technology shock that way, ask what it does to hours.

Here is that test, run in this film on American data from 1948 to 2019. With hours entered in growth rates, as Galí did, a technology improvement lowers hours, by 0.28 percent on impact, and the band of plausible answers is below zero throughout the first year. 100 percent of resampled histories agree. That is the opposite of the model. But in 2003 Lawrence Christiano, Martin Eichenbaum and Robert Vigfusson entered hours in levels instead, and hours rise: +0.15 percent on impact, climbing for a year, though with a band that reaches below zero. The two specifications disagree about everything that matters. In the first, technology explains about 9 percent of output's variance two years out; in the second, about 69. Which is right depends on whether hours have a trend that never reverses, which twenty years of argument have not settled. John Fernald showed in 2007 that allowing for breaks in productivity's trend growth pulls the levels result towards Galí's, and the corrected technology series of Basu, Fernald and Kimball also says hours fall.

The third front was money. The model has no money, so in it the central bank cannot matter at all. But Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz had shown that America's money supply fell by about a third between 1929 and 1933. Christina and David Romer, in 1989, read the Federal Reserve's own records to find the dates when it deliberately tightened to fight inflation, and found that output fell after each one. The recession of 1981 and 1982, the one where measured technology fell, was chosen by the central bank to end inflation. And housing, the spending most sensitive to interest rates, turns first. All of this says money and interest rates move output, and the next two parts build models in which they do.

Time for this part's forecast. Called it? In the autumn of 1986, Prescott wrote that technology shocks account for more than half of America's postwar fluctuations, with a best estimate near seventy-five percent, and in his theory a technology improvement raises output, investment and hours together. What happened: the measured shocks turned out to be partly not technology at all. Corrected for utilization, technology improvements cut hours at first. Long-run VARs split, as you just saw, depending on how hours enter. Partly right. Few economists now put technology's share near three quarters, and the mechanism through hours is in doubt. But technology does move the economy, and the way Prescott asked the question became the way everyone asks it.
Survived: So why did the method win? Because of what it left behind. Households and firms that optimize and look ahead, so that their behaviour does not change arbitrarily when policy does: Lucas's critique, answered. The whole economy solved at once, in equilibrium, with shocks inside. A computer to solve it, and the habit of comparing a model's simulated moments and impulse responses with the data's. And a place to put frictions when the data demand them: sticky prices, money, credit, search. The result is called a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model, and every central bank runs one. Kydland and Prescott shared the Nobel Prize in 2004, for this and for their work on time consistency.

The model also became a measuring instrument. In 2007, V. V. Chari, Patrick Kehoe and Ellen McGrattan proposed business cycle accounting. Keep the growth model, and let four wedges absorb everything it gets wrong. An efficiency wedge: how much output comes from given inputs. A labour wedge: a gap between what an hour is worth to the worker and to the firm, like a tax on work. An investment wedge: a gap between what savers want and what capital returns. And government spending. Measure the wedges from the data, feed them back one at a time, and see which one made each recession. Each wedge points to the kind of friction a better model needs.

Here is the labour wedge, computed in this film from three American series. It compares what an hour is worth to a worker in this model, set by consumption, with what an hour produces. If labour markets worked as the model says, the two would be equal, and the wedge would be zero. In pink, the wedge's gap from trend. In green, output's. They move against each other, with a correlation of minus 0.63. In every recession it is as if a tax on work suddenly rose. Robert Shimer set it out in 2009 as a challenge for every theory of the labour market. Wherever that friction lives, in wages that do not adjust or in the slow search of Part twenty-four, the growth model alone does not have it.

Other shocks joined technology. News: Paul Beaudry and Franck Portier showed in 2006 that stock prices jump on news about technology years before it arrives, and spending moves at once, so a boom can begin on expectations alone. Uncertainty: Nicholas Bloom showed in 2009 that when uncertainty jumps, firms pause hiring and investing, then rebound once it passes. Investment shocks: changes in how cheaply saving turns into capital, which in estimated models account for a large share of the cycle. The lesson is not one shock but many, with frictions, inside the framework Kydland and Prescott built.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the Frisch elasticity.

This part's new dial is the Frisch elasticity: how much people change their hours when the wage changes for a while. Raj Chetty, Adam Guren, Day Manoli and Andrea Weber gathered the evidence in 2011. For people who already work, changing how many hours they work: about point five four. For the decision whether to work at all: about point two eight. The two margins together, for hours in the whole economy: about point eight two. Against that, the value typical in macroeconomic models, as the same review reports it: about two point eight four. And this film's number: to make the Island's hours even half as volatile as its output, the elasticity must be about 2.1. The status: contested. Part of the gap closes by counting people who move in and out of work, and part remains. It decides whether a recession can be read as people choosing more leisure.

Why can the two numbers differ so much? Studies of individuals watch people whose wages change for a reason they can see, for a while, and measure how their hours respond. But in a whole economy, most of the movement in hours is people starting and losing jobs. Rogerson and Hansen showed that when jobs come in shifts, the economy's elasticity can be far larger than any single person's. The trouble is that people who lose their jobs in a recession say they did not choose to: unemployment is not leisure taken because wages fell for a while. That is why the parts on search and on sticky prices put frictions into the labour market instead.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: the model in the institution.

Two of the series' facts now get Agora's column. Investment is about three times as volatile as output, consumption less. In American data, investment moves 4.6 times as much as output, and consumption 0.77 times, durables included. The theory: households smooth consumption, spreading a temporary gain over years, so capital absorbs the swings. On the Island, investment moves 3.2 times as much as output and consumption 0.29: the right order, too smooth on both counts.

Hours rise in booms and fall in recessions: in the data they move 0.90 times as much as business output, with a correlation of 0.86. The theory: people work when work pays best. The Island gets the size, 0.76, with Hansen's help, but its hours move in lockstep with productivity, and America's do not. A fact can be matched for the wrong reason.

Where does this live now? In central banks. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York publishes the forecasts of its DSGE model; the European Central Bank, the Bank of England and Sweden's Riksbank run their own. Each is this part's model at its core, with sticky prices and wages, money, credit, and many shocks added. They are used for forecasts whose pieces add up, for a story behind each forecast, and for asking what would happen under a different policy. And they are solved with software like Dynare, free and open: you write down the equilibrium conditions, and it linearizes, solves and simulates exactly as chapter eight did by hand.

The modeller's job follows this part step by step. Write down the conditions: optimality, market clearing, and the shocks. Find the steady state, and make it match the long-run facts. Calibrate or estimate the parameters. Solve, by linearizing and counting the roots. Test the model's moments and responses against the data's, honestly, misses included. And only then use it: for a forecast, a scenario, or a policy question.
